chose: batch reports resolve through execNamedTest in phrasebook.ts, the single shared executable arm
over: a separate batch code path in verify.ts alongside the per-claim one
teaching each of the three executable claim forms about batching individually
because: 'passes test', 'boundary … via test' and 'parity … via test' ALREADY funnel every runner invocation through execNamedTest. Intercepting there means the batch inherits all three forms — including the expensive boundary oracles — with one edit, and the fallback is literally the untouched body of the same function. Three call sites taught separately would be three chances to diverge on what green means.

chose: mirror -t by literal substring on the report's fullName field
over: regex-matching the claim name against fullName
because: VERIFIED against vitest 4.1.10: -t is an UNANCHORED REGEX over fullName (ancestorTitles.join(' ')+' '+title). -t 'totality covers' matched 'write policy totality covers every op' — a substring spanning the describe/it boundary — and unescaped -t 'rejects unknown (a+b)' matched ZERO tests while the reEscape'd form matched one. Since the per-claim path always reEscapes first, an escaped-regex unanchored match IS exactly a literal substring test, so fullName.includes(name) is the precise mirror. Exact equality would silently red every claim anchored to a describe title rather than a full leaf name — the common case.

chose: support BOTH --outputFile and stdout, reading the file when the command carries --outputFile, and tolerating stdout via a brace-balanced scan for the last top-level object carrying testResults
over: stdout only with a whole-string JSON.parse
requiring --outputFile and erroring on a bare stdout command
because: MEASURED: a test doing process.stdout.write('RAW WRITE') put that text ahead of the report, and whole-file JSON.parse threw 'Unexpected token R'. vitest emits the report last, so the pollution observed was strictly BEFORE the JSON and a scan recovers it — but relying on that ordering for every consuming repo is a bet. --outputFile is immune (stdout dropped to 50 bytes, file parsed clean), so it is what the docs recommend; the stdout scan exists so the obvious ['npx','vitest','run','--reporter=json'] a reader will type first does not mysteriously fall back forever.

chose: green requires >=1 PASSED match and 0 failed, treating skipped matches as neither evidence nor failure
over: the literal brief wording 'every matching test passed', which would red a describe containing one it.skip
because: the mandate is to MIRROR the per-claim path, and mirroring beats the wording where they disagree. A describe with four its and one .skip: vitest -t <title> exits 0 with '4 passed | 1 skipped', testMatch '[1-9][0-9]* passed' matches, per-claim says GREEN. Requiring EVERY match to be passed would make batch STRICTER than the path it replaces and turn a config flip into a wave of new reds in repos that were honestly green. Requiring >=1 passed keeps the testMatch guarantee (positive evidence) without inventing a new one.

chose: record the batch marker RUN-level on VerifySection, not per-claim on ClaimRecord
over: a per-claim batched:true field alongside the verdict
because: checked mergeClaimRecords first, as instructed: its skip-doesn't-clobber branch does {...old}, so a per-claim marker would survive onto a verdict measured by the OTHER path in an earlier run — a provenance field that lies is worse than none. VerifySection is rewritten whole every run and takes part in no merge, so one field there is free of that hazard and reads correctly for scoped runs too. A verdict is a verdict; this sits next to commit/dirty as provenance about the instrument.

chose: treat only a non-running runner or an unparsable report as a batch crash; ignore the exit code entirely, and raise spawnSync maxBuffer to 64 MiB
over: treating a nonzero exit as a crash that triggers fallback
leaving maxBuffer at the spawnSync default
because: a suite with a red test exits nonzero, and that is exactly the run whose report is most worth reading — keying the fallback on exit status would fall back to the 30-minute path on every run that had a failure, i.e. precisely when you are iterating. The maxBuffer point is the same hazard by another route: the default is 1 MiB and a vitest JSON report embeds a full stack trace per failure, so the FAILING run is the one whose report arrives truncated and unparsable, which would have looked like a mysterious fallback that only ever happened when something was broken.

chose: add --from-report <file> as a third tier that reads a report an OUTER gate already produced
over: batch-only, where coherence always runs the suite itself
because: field data from a second consuming repo: their check.mjs already runs the whole suite, and coherence then ran it again — 17 targeted oracle runs at 4.51s each, of which '7 passed | 291 skipped' shows ~60s was pure import/transform cost for 298 tests to execute 7. Batch mode alone cuts 18 suite imports to 1; --from-report cuts it to ZERO, because the answer was already computed by the run that just finished. The flag is its own opt-in and needs no testBatch configured — the caller passing a path is asserting the file is current, which is a claim only the caller can make.

chose: name the zero-match verdict VANISHED ORACLE and treat three-state resolution as the feature, with speed as the side effect
over: reporting zero matches as a generic red
framing the whole feature as a performance optimization
because: the report distinguishes ran+passed, ran+failed, and DOES NOT EXIST. The per-claim path cannot see the third state — vitest -t exits 0 on a filter that matched nothing — so a renamed or deleted oracle reads as GREEN unless the project knew to configure testMatch. That is the same defect class as a typo'd claim verb: a hole plugged by a knob a reader has to know about. Batch mode observes absence directly, so testMatch has nothing left to do for a batched claim. A verdict named 'VANISHED ORACLE' says which of the three states it is; 'red' does not, and the distinction is the one that catches spec rot.

chose: keep the batch as shared EVIDENCE resolved per claim, never a shared verdict
over: one suite-level verdict applied to every executable claim
because: the per-claim path's best property is that each claim fails alone, naming its own oracle — that is what makes a red actionable instead of a summons to read the whole suite. Batching changes where the evidence comes from and nothing else: resolveFromBatch takes ONE name and returns ONE detail, so three claims over one report produce three independent verdicts (locked by a test asserting a green claim is not dragged down by two red neighbours sharing the report). Aggregating would have been simpler and would have been a regression.

chose: batching node:test consumers — no derivable format shipped in v0.17.0, so node:test is RECOGNIZED and refused with instructions rather than guessed at
because: measured on Node 25.2.1: node:test ships NO json reporter (node:test/reporters exports only default, dot, junit, lcov, spec, tap), so there is no report with a vitest-style concatenated fullName to read. Worse, its --test-name-pattern does NOT match a concatenated name — pattern 'outer group inner leaf' matched nothing while 'inner leaf' and 'outer group' each matched — so the vitest mirror (literal substring over fullName) would be WRONG for node:test, not merely unavailable. Parsing tap (nested sub-TAP) or junit (XML) is possible but the matching rule is a second semantic model, and shipping a mirror I have not verified is the one thing this feature is not allowed to do.

chose: node:test reports a PASSING entry named after the test FILE when --test-name-pattern matches nothing: pattern 'and +plus' over a file with no such test printed 'ok 1 - /tmp/nt-nested.test.ts', '# pass 1', and exited 0
couldBe: the instrument is wrong — the thing that PRODUCED this number, not the thing it describes

node:test treats the file-level subtest as the unit and marks it passed when it ran cleanly with zero matching descendants — so a vanished oracle is green AND a testMatch regex like '[1-9][0-9]* passed' is SATISFIED by it, making node:test consumers strictly more exposed to the vanished-oracle hole than vitest ones, where testMatch at least works
discriminatedBy: point a coherence 'passes test' claim at a name no node:test test has, with config.testMatch set to the README's recommended '[1-9][0-9]* passed', and see whether the claim goes green. If it does, the README's testMatch advice does not protect node:test projects at all and the batch path is the only real fix for them.

chose: make batch the DEFAULT full-tier path (deriving the command from config.test for vitest) and put the serial per-claim profile behind an explicit --serial-oracles / oracleExecution:"serial", refusing loudly when neither is available
over: the additive design shipped an hour earlier: feature OFF unless testBatch is configured, per coherence's own 'no behaviour change by default' discipline
keeping serial as the fallback default and merely documenting the cost
because: the additive design is right for a FEATURE and wrong for a DEFECT. 20-35 minutes to re-derive evidence one boot already contains is not a conservative default, it is a bad one nobody chose — and the measured second repo shows consumers do not discover the knob: they were paying the suite's import cost 18 times WHILE their own check.mjs paid it once. An opt-in fast path means the projects that most need it are the least likely to have it. Fail-closed is the harness's own doctrine applied to itself: a consumer must TYPE --serial-oracles to get the expensive profile, and an unknown runner refuses with three named ways out rather than silently choosing the worst one.

chose: prove the report file postdates the batch run (mtime vs a pre-spawn timestamp) and refuse a leftover one as stale
over: reading whatever is at the --outputFile path, as the first implementation did
because: found while chasing a suspiciously fast smoke run: if the runner exits WITHOUT writing (a config error, a collection failure) and a report from a previous run is still on disk, reading it resolves every claim from evidence about code that no longer exists — and it looks completely healthy. That is strictly worse than a crash, which at least falls back loudly. A pre-spawn timestamp plus statSync makes it structural. 2s of slack absorbs coarse filesystem mtime granularity and cannot admit a previous run's file.
